title: How do airlines make money, and what matters in an airline case?
description: Airline economics for case interviews: load factor, yield, cost per seat-mile, fixed costs and ancillary revenue, with a worked break-even load factor.
hook: Airlines make money by filling expensive, mostly fixed-cost flights with enough passengers at a high enough average fare, then adding fees for bags, seats and loyalty points. Margins are thin, so an airline case almost always comes down to three numbers: how full the planes are (load factor), what each passenger pays (yield) and what each seat costs to fly (unit cost).
body:
How an airline makes money

Most revenue is ticket sales. On top of that come ancillaries (checked bags, seat selection, food, priority boarding), cargo carried in the hold, and loyalty programmes, where banks buy miles or points from the airline to reward holders of co-branded credit cards.

The industry as a whole earns very little on all this. In its June 2026 outlook, IATA, the airline trade body, forecast a global net profit margin of about 2.0% for 2026, around $4.50 of profit per passenger, with fuel expected to be about 31% of operating costs as jet fuel prices rose (IATA press release).

The measures that matter

MeasureWhat it means
Available seat-miles (ASM)Seats flown × miles flown: the airline's capacity
Load factorShare of seats filled with paying passengers
YieldAverage passenger revenue per passenger-mile
RASMRevenue per available seat-mile (roughly load factor × yield)
CASMCost per available seat-mile, whether the seat is full or empty

The airline makes money when RASM is above CASM. Everything in an airline profitability case pushes one of those two numbers. Break-even load factor follows directly: it is the cost per seat divided by the revenue per passenger.

Why fixed costs dominate

Once a flight is scheduled, the aircraft, crew, airport and navigation charges, maintenance and most of the fuel cost roughly the same whether the plane is full or half empty. So the last few passengers on a flight are almost pure profit, and a small drop in load factor can wipe profit out. This is operating leverage in its purest form, and it is why airlines discount unsold seats close to departure rather than fly them empty.

A worked example: one route

An airline is considering a new daily departure on a 180-seat jet. Assume an average fare of $125, $15 of ancillary revenue per passenger and $18,000 of cost per departure (fuel, crew, landing charges, maintenance and an allocated share of the aircraft's ownership cost). These are illustrative numbers.

  • Revenue per passenger: $125 + $15 = $140.
  • At an 80% load factor: 180 × 80% = 144 passengers. Revenue = 144 × $140 = $20,160. Profit = $20,160 − $18,000 = $2,160 per departure, or about $788k a year over 365 departures.
  • Per seat: revenue per available seat is $20,160 ÷ 180 = $112, against a cost per seat of $18,000 ÷ 180 = $100.
  • Break-even: $18,000 ÷ $140 = 128.6 passengers, so a break-even load factor of 128.6 ÷ 180 = 71.4%. Without the ancillaries it would be $18,000 ÷ $125 = 144 passengers, or 80%. The extras lower break-even by almost nine points.

Now test sensitivity. If load factor drops from 80% to 75%, the flight loses 9 passengers × $140 = $1,260, which is 58% of its profit. At 70%, revenue is 126 × $140 = $17,640 and the flight loses $360. If fuel is 30% of the cost ($5,400) and fuel prices rise 20%, cost rises by $1,080 and profit halves to $1,080.

Before recommending the launch, you would want a monthly forecast of passengers and fares (is demand seasonal?), whether the airline has slots and a spare aircraft, and whether the route feeds connecting passengers or simply takes customers from the airline's existing flights.

What a strong answer sounds like

Weak: "Revenue per passenger is up, so pricing is fine. I'd look at costs."
Strong: "Revenue per passenger is up, but I'd compare revenue per seat with cost per seat. If we raised fares and load factor fell from 85% to 76%, revenue per seat could have dropped even though each passenger pays more."

The strong version uses the airline's own measures and gives a testable hypothesis.

Typical airline case questions

  • Why did we lose money when passenger numbers rose? (fares, mix, fuel, capacity growth)
  • Should we launch a new route? (demand, yield, cost per flight, competition, slots)
  • How can we grow ancillary or loyalty revenue?
  • Why are our planes slower to turn around, or slower through maintenance, than rivals'? (an operations case)

Common mistakes

  • Thinking per passenger instead of per seat. Empty seats cost almost as much as full ones. Always bring revenue back to RASM or revenue per seat.
  • Forgetting ancillaries and loyalty. They can move break-even load factor by several points.
  • Treating aircraft cost as variable. For a decision about next month's schedule, the plane is already paid for. For a decision about the fleet, it is not. Say which horizon you mean.
  • Looking at one route in isolation. A loss-making route may feed profitable connections. Ask how many passengers connect onward before cutting it.

Practise

1. A 150-seat flight costs $15,000 to operate. The average fare is $100 and ancillaries add $20 per passenger. What is the break-even load factor?

Show the answer

Revenue per passenger is $120. Break-even passengers = $15,000 ÷ $120 = 125. Break-even load factor = 125 ÷ 150 = 83.3%. That is high, so the route only works if it reliably fills well above that.

2. Airline A fills 85% of seats at a yield of 12 cents per passenger-mile. Airline B fills 78% at 14 cents. Which earns more passenger revenue per seat-mile?

Show the answer

A: 85% × 12 cents = 10.2 cents. B: 78% × 14 cents = 10.92 cents. B earns more per seat-mile despite flying emptier planes. Whether B is more profitable depends on its cost per seat-mile.

3. A carrier's revenue per passenger has risen, but route profit has fallen. What three explanations would you investigate first?

Show the answer

(1) Load factor fell, so revenue per seat dropped even as each passenger paid more. (2) Costs per seat rose, most likely fuel, or crew and maintenance if aircraft fly fewer hours a day. (3) Capacity changed: a larger aircraft or extra frequencies added seats faster than demand. Ask for revenue and cost per seat before suggesting any fare change.

Where to practise next

Try the full Northline Air case, where passenger numbers rose but the airline lost money, and the SkyLine MRO case on maintenance turnaround. For the maths, the break-even shortcut and unit economics cover the tools you need, and the maths drills build speed.
